name: Venezia-Murano-Burano
text: Italian press coverage of Venice's historic-center Municipalità is dominated by one very well-documented issue: pickpocketing and petty theft targeting tourists in the most crowded zones — Piazza San Marco, the Rialto Bridge/market area, the Accademia bridge, and the corridor between the train station and Cannaregio/Strada Nova. Il Gazzettino and La Nuova Venezia have run repeated 2024-2025 stories on organized pickpocket crews (including one alley nicknamed "Calle Pickpocket"), gondoliers physically intervening to stop thieves, and municipal figures citing roughly 50-130 pickpockets stopped by local police within months in 2025. There are also documented, if less frequent, muggings/assaults on tourists (a bag-snatching that hospitalized a victim with concussion in September 2024, an aggression near Rialto, a pickpocket who beat a victim who caught her) and a June 2026 ANSA report on unofficial "porters" arrested for extortion/threats against tourists at the station. A September 2025 Sky TG24 report described Jewish tourists verbally and physically harassed. Classic overcharging scams (inflated restaurant bills) are also frequently reported. Separately, Cannaregio (especially near the station) has seen residents protest with anti-drug-dealing banners, prefecture-ordered interforze patrols, and police drug seizures through 2025; nearby Fondamenta della Misericordia has prompted bar-hour ordinances over rowdy nightlife noise. No credible, dated reporting ties any of this to Giudecca, Murano or Burano beyond isolated shop burglaries (a Murano glass-shop safe-crack, an attempted Burano jewelry-store theft) — these islands show no documented pattern of tourist-directed crime and default to no particular concern. Violent crime overall remains rare; Venice's international reputation as a very safe destination is intact, though petty theft is genuinely common enough in the tourist core to warrant caution both day and night.

name: Lido-Pellestrina
text: Genuine Italian press coverage (Il Gazzettino, La Nuova Venezia, VeneziaToday, La Voce di Venezia) from 2024-2026 shows Lido-Pellestrina remains a low-crime, mostly residential and resort area with no pattern of violent crime, muggings, or organized theft targeting tourists comparable to Venice's historic center. The main documented issue is opportunistic petty theft at Lido's beach establishments: a recurring pattern of bags, cash, credit cards, and keys stolen from beach umbrellas/cabins while owners swim (e.g. a Milan couple robbed of 500 euros and keys at a beach club in August 2025; a serial thief repeatedly targeting cabins at two well-known beaches), and occasional break-ins into parked cars near the vaporetto stops with thieves fleeing by boat. Venice Local Police ran a "Spiagge Sicure" enforcement operation on Lido beaches in July 2026, though it targeted illegal vendors, not violent crime. Drug-related arrests occur occasionally on Lido but at a level consistent with any Italian town, not a hotspot. A genuine, separate safety concern is traffic/pedestrian risk on Lido's main artery, Via Sandro Gallo, where at least two elderly pedestrians were struck and killed by vehicles in recent incidents (2024-2025) — a road-safety issue rather than crime. No evidence was found of nightlife violence, assault, harassment, or any notable crime pattern specific to Pellestrina, which press coverage confirms is a quiet fishing community; searches turned up only routine administrative/labor-safety checks there. Given the absence of violent crime or theft targeting people after dark, both day and night default to no particular concern, with the main practical caution being standard beach-bag vigilance and pedestrian care on the main road.

name: Marghera
text: Italian press from 2024-2025 documents recurring, localized problems in Marghera rather than widespread violent crime. Drug dealing is the most consistently reported issue: La Nuova Venezia described tram stops used for street dealing (February 2024) and "drug riders" delivering to busy squares and parks, while Il Gazzettino reported a construction worker arrested with 7kg of cocaine hidden in a Marghera garage, and other pieces cite multiple arrests for spaccio in Mestre-Marghera. VeneziaToday reported 425 police citations issued in Marghera during 2024 tied to security/degrado/spaccio checks. Il Gazzettino explicitly flagged Mestre-Marghera districts as riskier after dark, and residents have staged public protests over degrado and drug dealing around the pedestrian underpass linking Marghera to Mestre, prompting mayoral night walkthroughs. A notable 2025 incident: on 22 March a brawl involving roughly 60 mostly-underage youths broke out at the Nave de Vero shopping center, leading the Prefettura to declare a temporary enhanced-security zone around the mall. Older housing blocks in the Quartiere Cita area reflect long-standing post-industrial socioeconomic decline, with redevelopment funding reported by VeneziaToday. No sources found evidence of frequent violent street crime, muggings of tourists, or no-go areas for ordinary daytime visitors; concerns center on specific spots (the underpass, the mall, tram stops) and are more pronounced at night.

name: Mestre-Carpenedo
text: Multiple current Italian outlets document a persistent, geographically concentrated problem in the Mestre train station corridor — Piazzale Cialdini, Via Piave, and the adjacent public gardens/underpass linking Mestre to Marghera — rather than across the whole Municipalità. Il Gazzettino, La Nuova Venezia and VeneziaToday have repeatedly reported open-air drug dealing there, and police "Alto Impatto" sweeps have identified dozens of people and made arrests in Via Piave specifically. A February 2026 La Nuova Venezia piece quotes Mestre residents describing worsening conditions, daylight drug transactions, changed routines (children's routes altered, no watches or cash carried) and a condo installing night gates after 15 years of requests. Night-time violence is also documented with real specifics: ANSA (26 February 2025) reported five arrests for a string of armed robberies/stabbings in the Marghera-Mestre underpass over Christmas/New Year (knife attacks, a dog set on a victim, bottle assault); ANSA also covered a July 2025 life sentence for a fatal attempted-robbery case in Mestre and a December 2025 robbery of an elderly resident. Authorities responded in 2025 with security turnstiles at Mestre station and prefect-led security meetings with Via Piave residents over burglaries. Carpenedo/Bissuola residential streets showed only a scattered 2023 burglary spree with no comparable recent pattern — those areas otherwise lack documented ongoing concern and are calmer than the station corridor. The concentrated, dated, repeated nature of the station-corridor incidents (drug dealing, armed robbery, stabbings) supports a red night rating for the district overall, while daytime risk is real but more limited to specific spots.

name: Chirignago-Zelarino
text: This mainland residential municipalità (Chirignago, Zelarino, Gazzera, Cipressina, Trivignano) produced no evidence of a serious or ongoing crime wave in recent press coverage, and daytime life for residents and visitors appears unremarkable. The most substantive dated find is a Guardia di Finanza drug bust in Chirignago on 16 January 2026, where a man was arrested after police found over 700g of heroin, cocaine and hashish plus cash in what La Nuova Venezia described as a small drug-dealing operation — consistent with an earlier, larger 2021 Polizia Locale operation that dismantled a heroin-dealing point in the Zelarino countryside (900 doses seized). In 2026 Chirignago residents, mostly elderly, were also targeted by scammers posing as utility technicians to enter homes and steal valuables, part of a wider Mestre-area trend. VeneziaToday also reported a spate of car windows and windscreens smashed in a single raid in Cipressina. Notably, a March 2024 scare in Gazzera — a large police response to reported gunshots — turned out to be a false alarm with no victim or weapon found. No pattern of street robbery, assault, or organized violence specific to this district (as distinct from central Mestre or Venice's historic center) was found. Overall this reads as a quiet suburban area with only isolated, mostly non-violent, drug- and property-related incidents, warranting a cautious yellow at night rather than green given the documented drug operations.

name: Favaro Veneto
text: Extensive searches of Il Gazzettino, La Nuova Venezia, VeneziaToday, La Piazza Web, and Antenna Tre/Medianordest turned up no pattern of muggings, tourist-targeted pickpocketing, or organized crime in Favaro Veneto, Campalto or Dese — unlike central Venice, which has well-documented tourist-theft problems. The most significant dated finding is a real, resolved 2026 case: starting after Easter, a 40-year-old Favaro resident carried out a months-long stalking and intimidation campaign against a relative, including death threats, a garage arson, and setting fire to a well-known local baker's car; press described the neighbourhood as feeling under siege until his arrest in August 2026. Older, dated items (2019-2022) show isolated but real incidents — a drug-dealing operation broken up at a hotel, a knife altercation in the pedestrian square, an armed-robbery suspect arrested hiding in a Favaro apartment, and a violent multi-vehicle chase with reported gunshots near Campalto's Via Orlanda in December 2022 — but nothing recurring or current enough to indicate an ongoing hotspot. Regional data shows Veneto ranks second nationally for home burglaries in 2024, a province-wide trend rather than a Favaro-specific one. Overall this is a quiet, largely residential and airport-adjacent district with no daytime safety concerns found; night is marked yellow reflecting the genuine, recent (2026) arson/stalking episode and the region's elevated home-burglary backdrop, not any pattern of street crime against residents or visitors.
